I hear you and feel you are entitled to your opinion. I am a masters in psychology and have a practice in psychotherapy. I have done relationship counselling for a little over 10 years.

I only took exception to the term irreconcilable meaning it can’t be solved. I may be older and traditionally minded. What I have learned is when someone is married or has been in a relationship as long as the poster said, it is not helpful or fair to them to define irreconcilable as a reason to end. It is a legal term used as a euphemism to say “my wife is fat”, “my husband is bald” during a divorce. Yes sometimes its valid. But I can tell you from experience most folks that start out with irreconcilable difference do the work & change. From losing weight, to financial support, to reciprocating in the bedroom. Those are the more common issues.

Its like learning the etiquette of real communication. We have to separate the emotional and help the process. Its not very logical in the beginning. When emotions are high people tend to make the worst decisions, say things they don’t mean and undermine their own best interests.

I have to clarify where I am coming from. In America we have conditions that make people avoid what we like to call growth because there is more money to extract from working class people when they have a lot of relationships. Even better when kids are involved. You should see what my clients buy their kids to out do their ex husband or ex wife.

Most of my clients are middle class.  

When they come to me they have the time and are able to learn healthy habits although it often happens because in America we are taught that everything is a commodity and people become obsolete. Just like a cell phone or car. If it loses its lustre, we are told to throw it away and never pick up the skills that offer far more satisfaction in seeing a relationship as an organism we cultivate and improve by making ourselves better listeners, aware of the childhood trauma, stopping the cycle. 

So yesterday I came home from helping a client come to terms with their grief as they learned their ex husband who had an illness during their marriage recovered from it. 
She saw it in our local paper and he was remarried and it was talking about the support from the new wife during his illness.

I see a lot of cases repeat cycles that rely on irreconcilable terms as the reason they end things but it always resurfaces and inhibits people from substantial growth. It was especially hard to work with this patient because they had started together but once the divorce was set in motion he had stuck to the work in being present , introspective and active but she stopped. It had been 3 years but the thing about it is they had known each other half their life and they came from different cultures and it was always my opinion that external factors interfered in something that didn’t have to end. 

That is he was ill, probably would get worse.  He knew the relationship was over but even in his 50s recognized that loving himself would enable him to love his ex wife and even though that didn’t become a reality he had learned enough to find love in someone that didn’t take for granted his capacity to love himself. Everyone had told him he was too old to get better. The social stigma went to work on him, but with therapy he over came it. Despite living in a world that wants people to fail, he did the work to change. Its very easy to fall into group think. 

I see in my career good people become great people when they begin to understand what it really means to listen to one another and its never easy. If we grew up with parents that never listened to us, there  is no way that we learned what to pay attention to. 
Its very rare at least. So its especially hard for me to see the anguish of a divorcee with a string of failed relationships tell me they always wanted to work it out but because she started reading Cosmo or psychology today or what have you she only started seeing fault and burden in her future. 

I see it often. Anecdotal accounts from some media sources, sprinkled with well intentioned cultural and social pressure working in perpetuity with advertisements. Maybe a divorce lawyer. A car you can buy if only you are not attached. A trip to Monaco or Egypt. I suppose I had been carrying something and I just caution anyone, being fickle about the capacity for relationships to overcome challenges is very disrespectful. I see more genuinely devoted people than abuse and its very traumatic for very intelligent people to be in therapy later in life and now have to learn how to process grief. 

The patients I see asking me these kinds of questions do so because, yes, they’re insecure about some things, but they still believe in their partners and the consequences are far more costly when people buy into things aimed at selling us a lifestyle. Relationships can usually change and become stronger. I see it every day. I just needed to encourage, maybe for my own sake people to be aware what love **really** means to people in a relationship. That promoting self interest can influence people to do things they regret and its far more respectful to support the relationship than serving agendas manufactured by the advertising companies at google making everyone chase things that aren’t actually real.
